mcqs.question: What is the main hardware problem with sign-magnitude representation?
options: It cannot represent negative numbers at all
It has two representations of zero and needs extra logic beyond plain addition
It uses more bits than two's complement for the same range
It only works for even numbers
mcqs.explanation: Sign-magnitude has both +0 and -0 as distinct bit patterns, and a plain adder gives wrong answers when signs differ, so extra sign-checking logic is needed. It represents negatives fine — the issue is arithmetic cost, not representability.

mcqs.question: What makes two's complement addition work with a plain unsigned adder, with no special-casing?
options: Two's complement numbers are always positive internally
Overflow bits are simply discarded, and the invert-and-add-1 encoding makes the sum come out correct mod 2^n
The CPU checks the sign bits first and routes to a different circuit
Two's complement avoids using the top bit entirely
mcqs.explanation: Two's complement is defined so that adding any two encoded values and truncating to the register width (discarding overflow) always gives the mathematically correct result mod 2^n — no sign-checking circuit is needed, unlike sign-magnitude or one's complement.

mcqs.question: Why is the signed 8-bit range -128 to 127 instead of -127 to 127?
options: It's an arbitrary choice made by early compiler designers
Two's complement has a single zero, leaving one 'extra' bit pattern that gets assigned to the most negative value with no positive counterpart
8-bit registers actually have 257 possible states
127 is reserved as an error code, not an actual value
mcqs.explanation: 256 total bit patterns, one used for zero, leaves 255 split between signs — but that split is uneven because one pattern (the top bit set, rest zero) is used for -128 with no matching +128.

mcqs.question: Why did hardware designers standardize on two's complement over one's complement, given both encode negatives similarly (bit flipping)?
options: Two's complement uses fewer bits per number
Two's complement removes both the double-zero problem and the end-around-carry correction step, needing simpler adder hardware
One's complement cannot represent negative numbers larger than -4
Two's complement was mandated by an early ISO standard, not a hardware efficiency reason
mcqs.explanation: The deciding factor was circuit simplicity: two's complement needs no carry-correction logic and has only one zero, so it needs strictly less hardware than one's complement for the same job.

mcqs.question: What happens when you negate INT_MIN (the most negative representable value) in two's complement?
options: It correctly produces the largest positive value
It wraps back around to the same negative value, since there's no positive counterpart in that width
It raises a hardware exception on every CPU
It becomes zero
mcqs.explanation: Because the range is asymmetric, the most negative value has no matching positive value in the same bit width, so invert-and-add-1 lands back on the same bit pattern — this is why negating or taking abs() of INT_MIN is a classic undefined-behavior bug in C/C++.
